hints: Think about the bond angle around each carbon in benzene and what this tells you about the overall shape of the six carbon ring.
Recall the hybridisation of carbon in benzene and which orbitals overlap head on to make the C-C and C-H framework.
Consider what is left over on each carbon after sigma bonding and how these orbitals overlap to create the pi system.
walkthrough:
Picture the sigma framework first**
Think of benzene as a flat hexagon. Each carbon uses three $\text{sp}^2$ hybrid orbitals arranged at $120^{\circ}$ in one plane. Two of these overlap with neighbouring carbons and one overlaps with hydrogen to make strong $\sigma$ bonds. This head on overlap is what locks the molecule flat.

Spot the leftover p orbital**
After making three sigma bonds, each carbon still has one unhybridised p orbital sticking up and down at right angles to the plane of the ring. These p orbitals do not point at each other, so they cannot make sigma bonds.

Build the pi cloud by sideways overlap**
Each p orbital overlaps sideways with the p orbitals on both neighbours, above and below the plane. Because all six overlap together, the six $\pi$ electrons are not fixed in three double bonds but are delocalised around the whole ring. This delocalisation plus the $120^{\circ}$ $\text{sp}^2$ arrangement explains why benzene is perfectly planar.

Final answer: Benzene is planar hexagonal with bond angle $120^{\circ}$.
Each C is $\text{sp}^2$ hybridised, $\text{sp}^2$ orbitals overlap head on to form $\sigma$ bonds (C-C and C-H).
One unhybridised p orbital on each C overlaps sideways above and below the ring to form a delocalised $\pi$ system.

hints: Remember that concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acts as a strong acid toward $\text{HNO}_3$ to generate the powerful electrophile $\text{NO}_2^+$.
walkthrough:
Identify the real attacker**
In nitration the benzene ring does not react with $\text{HNO}_3$ itself. The strong acid $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ protonates $\text{HNO}_3$, which then loses water to leave the nitronium ion, $\text{NO}_2^+$. That positive ion is the electrophile that the pi cloud will attack.
Final answer: $\text{HNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + \text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Start the mechanism with the delocalised pi electrons of 1,2-dimethylbenzene attacking the positively charged N in $\text{NO}_2^+$.
Draw the resulting positively charged arenium intermediate with the $\text{NO}_2$ group attached and the positive charge delocalised in the ring.
Think about how aromaticity is restored by removal of the ring $\text{H}^+$ from the same carbon that now bears $\text{NO}_2$.
walkthrough:
First attack by the ring**
Picture the pi cloud of 1,2-dimethylbenzene as electron rich. Draw a curly arrow starting in the centre of the ring and pointing to the N atom of $\text{NO}_2^+$. The N is positive and electron poor, so a new C-N bond forms and the aromaticity is temporarily broken.

Draw the Wheland intermediate**
You now have a cyclohexadienyl cation. The $\text{NO}_2$ group is sigma bonded to one ring carbon which also still bears its H. The positive charge is delocalised over the other ring carbons. Show the + charge in the ring and the disrupted circle.

Restore aromaticity by deprotonation**
A base removes the $\text{H}^+$ from the carbon bearing the $\text{NO}_2$ group. Draw a curly arrow from that C-H bond back into the ring to reform the delocalised pi system. This gives product M, nitro-1,2-dimethylbenzene, plus $\text{H}^+$.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene $\pi$ system to N of $\text{NO}_2^+$ forming arenium cation intermediate with $\text{NO}_2$ attached and + charge in ring.
Curly arrow from C-H bond at site of substitution back into ring to reform aromatic $\pi$ system, $\text{H}^+$ lost to give M.

hints: Look at what was left from step (b)(i) and what was released in step (b)(ii) to see how $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ can be remade.
walkthrough:
Close the catalytic loop**
Step 1 made $\text{HSO}_4^-$ when $\text{NO}_2^+$ was formed, and step 2 released $\text{H}^+$ when aromaticity was restored. Those two combine to regenerate $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, which is why $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a catalyst and not used up.
Final answer: $\text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$

hints: Identify the functional group change in step 2 from $\text{NO}_2$ in M to $\text{NH}_2$ in 2,3-dimethylphenylamine.
Recall the classic A Level reagent for reducing an aromatic nitro group in acidic conditions.
walkthrough:
Recognise nitro to amine**
Compare M and the product. The $\text{NO}_2$ group has become $\text{NH}_2$. Nitrogen has gained hydrogen and lost oxygen, so this is a reduction that needs a powerful reducing agent in acid.

Recall the standard recipe**
For aromatic nitro compounds the textbook method is tin metal with concentrated hydrochloric acid and heat, $\text{Sn}$ / conc. $\text{HCl}$. Alternative $\text{Fe}$ / conc. $\text{HCl}$ is also accepted. This supplies hydrogen for the reduction to the primary aromatic amine.

Final answer: Reagents and conditions: $\text{Sn}$ + concentrated $\text{HCl}$ with heat, followed by alkaline work up.
Type of reaction: reduction.

hints: Count all carbons, hydrogens, nitrogens and oxygens carefully in the displayed structure of mefenamic acid, remembering H on the NH and $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups.
walkthrough:
Count atom by atom**
Two benzene rings give $12$ carbons, plus two $\text{CH}_3$ groups plus one $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ carbon gives $15$ carbons in total. Counting all ring H, methyl H, N-H and O-H gives $15$ hydrogens, with $1$ N and $2$ O. So the formula is $\text{C}_{15}\text{H}_{15}\text{NO}_2$.

hints: Look at the N-H link between the two rings and the $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group on the right hand ring.
walkthrough:
Name what you see**
The nitrogen joining the two aryl groups with one H attached is a secondary amine. The $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ group is a carboxylic acid. Benzene rings are to be ignored as instructed.
Final answer: Amine (secondary amine) and carboxylic acid.

hints: Calculate the moles of 2,3-dimethylphenylamine used from mass $5.00$ g and its $M_r$ of $121$.
Use the 1 to 1 mole ratio in the equation and the $M_r$ of mefenamic acid, $241$, to find the maximum mass.
walkthrough:
Find moles of limiting amine**
The other reagent is in excess, so the amine limits the yield. $$\text{moles} = \frac{\text{mass}}{M_r} = \frac{5.00}{121} = 0.04132 \text{ mol}$$ Keep extra figures for now.

Convert to mass of product**
The equation shows $1$ mol amine gives $1$ mol mefenamic acid. $$\text{mass} = \text{moles} \times M_r = 0.04132 \times 241 = 9.96 \text{ g}$$ Give the answer to three significant figures as requested.

Final answer: Moles amine $= 5.00 / 121 = 0.0413$ mol.
Moles mefenamic acid $= 0.0413$ mol, mass $= 0.0413 \times 241 = 9.96$ g (3 s.f.).

hints: Compare the type of carbocation intermediate formed by attack at the 2 and 4 positions versus attack at the 3 position.
Think about how the methyl group can donate electron density to a nearby positive charge and stabilise it.
walkthrough:
Sort the intermediates by substitution**
Look at the three cations drawn. When $\text{Br}$ adds at the 2 or 4 position, one resonance form places the positive charge on the carbon that already bears the $\text{CH}_3$ group. That carbon is attached to three carbons, so it is a tertiary carbocation. Attack at the 3 position never puts the + charge on that carbon, so the intermediate stays secondary.

Link alkyl donation to stability**
A $\text{CH}_3$ group pushes electron density toward a neighbouring positive centre through its positive inductive effect. This spreads and stabilises the charge, lowering the energy of the intermediate and the activation energy leading to it. So the 2 and 4 pathways are faster and the $\text{CH}_3$ group is 2,4 directing.

Final answer: Attack at 2 and 4 positions gives a more stable tertiary carbocation intermediate whereas attack at 3 position gives a less stable secondary carbocation.
Methyl / alkyl groups have a positive inductive (electron donating) effect which stabilises the positive charge.
